title: MRI Quench Vent Signs
guide:
Where quench vent signs go

  • At the vent outlet. A DANGER sign facing anyone who walks up to the discharge on the roof, an exterior wall or a courtyard.
  • Around the clear zone. Mark the area your MRI vendor's site planning drawings and your MR safety officer define, so nobody stages equipment, parks a lift or takes a break there.
  • At the roof hatch or door that leads to the vent, so contractors know before they step out.
  • Along the vent pipe where it runs through ceilings, chases and mechanical rooms, so nobody cuts it, crushes it or hangs something from it.
  • In the magnet room, post-quench instructions for staff: get out, keep the door open, call for help.

Why the vent matters

A quench turns liquid helium into gas very fast, and helium expands to hundreds of times its liquid volume. The plume at the outlet is cold enough to cause frostbite and displaces the oxygen around it. If the pipe is blocked by water, ice, debris or a crushed section, gas can back up into the magnet room instead. That is why MRI vendors and MR safety inspectors recommend checking the vent pathway at least once a year and keeping the discharge area posted and clear.

The people most likely to be near the outlet during a quench are the ones least likely to know an MRI sits under them: roofing crews, rooftop unit techs, window washers and firefighters.

Picking the signal word

Use DANGER at the outlet and the clear zone, where a quench can injure or kill someone standing there. Use WARNING or NOTICE labels for the pipe route and for procedures, where the message is about what not to do to the pipe or what to do after an event.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

  • MRI Suite sign kit, 8 signs
  • All hospital sign kits

Common questions

Is a quench vent sign required by law?

No single federal rule spells out quench vent wording. Posting the vent exit is a widely recommended practice in MRI site planning and inspection, and the details come from your MRI vendor's site planning guide and your facility's MR safety program.

How far should people stay from the outlet?

The clear zone depends on the vent design and location. Use the distance in your MRI vendor's site planning documents, and post the boundary so contractors can see it.

Will these signs hold up on a roof?

Yes. They are 8x12 inch .065 rust-resistant aluminum with UV-stable inks and pre-drilled corners, made for outdoor use and covered by a 5-year outdoor warranty.

Can you make a sign with our facility's emergency number?

Yes. Custom signs are priced close to catalog signs. Send us the wording and we will send a proof.

title: MRI Safety Signs
guide:
How MRI zone signs are laid out

Most MRI suites follow the four-zone layout from the American College of Radiology's guidance on MR safety:

  • Zone I: areas open to the public, outside the MR environment.
  • Zone II: the interface where patients are screened, under supervision of MR staff.
  • Zone III: restricted. Only screened people, under the control of MR personnel. Post the entry so nobody wanders in with a phone, oxygen tank or tool cart.
  • Zone IV: the scanner room itself. The magnet is always on, even when nobody is being scanned.

Where to post

  • Every door into Zone III and Zone IV, at eye level on the approach side.
  • Where the magnetic field extends beyond the scan room walls, including rooms above and below.
  • At equipment parking and storage, so MR Unsafe items stay out.
  • At the quench vent outlet and roof access. See MRI quench vent signs.
  • At the magnet room for post-quench and emergency procedures.

Who the signs are really for

MR staff know the rules. The signs are for everyone else: environmental services, facilities and biomed staff, contractors, security, transport and firefighters responding to an alarm. Many MRI projectile accidents involve staff or responders who did not realize the magnet is always on.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

  • MRI Suite sign kit, 8 signs
  • All hospital sign kits

Common questions

Do MRI zone signs have to say specific words?

There is no federally mandated wording. The ACR four-zone model is the common reference, and many facilities adopt it in their MR safety policy. Match your signs to that policy.

Is the magnet really always on?

For superconducting MRI systems, yes. The static magnetic field stays on when the scanner is idle and when the lights are off.

Do you make a full set for one suite?

Yes. The MRI Suite sign kit covers the zone doors, magnetic field warnings and quench vent in one order.

title: MRI Magnetic Field and Pacemaker Signs
guide:
Where these signs go

  • At every door into a magnet room or MRI Zone IV.
  • At the 5 gauss line, the boundary commonly used for pacemaker safety, wherever it falls outside the magnet room, including floors above and below.
  • At equipment parking, so oxygen cylinders, carts, chairs and tools that are MR Unsafe stay out.
  • On NMR and research magnet lab doors, where visitors and service staff come and go.

What the hazards are

Projectiles. A ferrous object brought near a strong magnet can be pulled in with enough force to injure anyone in the way. Implants. Pacemakers, defibrillators, neurostimulators and some other implants can be affected by strong fields. Equipment. MR Safe, MR Conditional and MR Unsafe labels follow ASTM F2503; the signs at the door tell people to check before they enter.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

  • MRI Suite sign kit, 8 signs
  • Laboratory sign kits

Common questions

Where is the 5 gauss line?

It depends on the magnet and the room shielding. Your MRI or magnet vendor's site plans show it. Post signs where people could cross it without knowing.

Are these only for hospitals?

No. Research NMR labs, university physics labs and plants with lifting magnets use the same warnings.

Full guide: MRI suite signage guide

title: Electric Shock Drowning and Marina Electrical Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At the head of every powered dock and along walkways, facing people on the dock.
  • Facing the water approach, so swimmers and boaters can read it.
  • At shore power pedestals and boat lift disconnects.
  • At lake homes and community docks where kids swim.

What the code says

The National Electrical Code added a signage requirement for marinas and boatyards in Article 555, calling for permanent signs that warn of possible shock hazard in the water. Many states and local authorities enforce it at inspection. Our electric shock drowning guide covers the details.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

  • Boat dock and marina kit
  • Marina and fuel dock kit, 8 signs
  • Port and marine sign kits

Common questions

Does electric shock drowning happen in salt water?

It is mainly a fresh water hazard. Fresh water conducts poorly, so the body becomes the easier path for current.

Is a sign enough?

No. A sign keeps people out of the water. The fix is inspection, ground fault protection and maintenance of dock and boat wiring by a qualified electrician.

Full guide: Electric shock drowning: what marinas need to post

guide:
Where to post

title: EV Service and High-Voltage Vehicle Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At the EV service bay, facing the shop floor.
  • On a stand or cone at the vehicle while the high-voltage system is being worked on.
  • At damaged battery storage and quarantine areas.
  • At EV chargers in the shop and in the lot.

Why it matters

EV and hybrid battery packs stay energized after the car is switched off. Manufacturers' service procedures call for disabling and verifying the high-voltage system before work, and for keeping untrained people away while it is exposed. A damaged pack can also go into thermal runaway hours or days later.

title: Drowning Hazard and Deep Water Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At every gate and access path to the water.
  • Along fences and banks, spaced so one is always in view.
  • At spillways, outfalls and intakes, where current can pull a person under.
  • At boat ramps and fishing access points for drop-offs and thin ice.

Who owns the risk

Cities, HOAs, water utilities, quarries and property managers own most of these sites, and the people at risk are usually kids and fishermen who never saw a safety talk. A clear DANGER sign at each approach is the simplest step in showing the hazard was posted.

Signing a whole site?

  • Public works sign kits

At least one at every access point, plus enough along the fence or bank that one is always in sight. Large sites order in 10 or 20 packs to get the quantity discount.

title: Blasting Area and Explosives Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At every road and path into the blast area, before the guard position.
  • On magazine doors and fences.
  • At detonator and cap storage, kept apart from explosives.
  • Where radio transmitters and cell phones must be turned off near electric initiation.

Standards to know

OSHA's construction blasting rules (29 CFR 1926 Subpart U), MSHA rules for mines and ATF storage rules all touch on posting and access control. Public road signs for blasting zones follow the MUTCD. Our signs cover the site and storage side, not highway traffic signs.

title: Emergency Assembly Point Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At the assembly point itself, high enough to see over a crowd.
  • Along the route from each exit, so people do not have to guess.
  • A second assembly point for when the first is downwind of a release or blocked.

Why it matters

An emergency action plan under OSHA 1910.38 has to include a way to account for everyone after an evacuation. A posted assembly point is how that plan works at 2 a.m. with a new hire and a contractor on site.

title: Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At hatches and entries to wet wells, vaults, manholes and digesters.
  • At tank battery gates and thief hatches.
  • Where personal H2S monitors are required, at the point people enter.
  • At wind socks and muster points on sour gas sites.

Why it is so dangerous

H2S smells like rotten eggs at low levels, but at higher levels it deadens the sense of smell, so people think the gas is gone. It is heavier than air and collects in low spaces. Many H2S fatalities are would-be rescuers who go in after a coworker without supplied air.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

  • Lift station kit, 8 signs
  • Process module and H2S kit, 4 signs
  • Oil and gas sign kits

Common questions

Is H2S signage required?

OSHA does not have a single H2S sign rule, but confined space and hazard communication rules require warning and training where H2S is present. Posted signs are the standard practice at wastewater and oilfield sites.

Do you make H2S signs with a monitor requirement?

Yes, several, and we make custom versions too.

Full guide: Permit-required confined space posting

title: Oxygen Deficiency and Cryogenic Gas Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At the door to rooms with cryogenic storage or inert gas systems.
  • At dewar fill stations and bulk tank fill points.
  • Where an oxygen monitor alarm means leave now.
  • At pits and low areas where cold gas settles.

Why it matters

OSHA treats air with less than 19.5% oxygen as oxygen deficient. A small liquid nitrogen spill in a closed room can push oxygen well below that, and the first symptom can be collapse. Cryogenic liquids also cause severe cold burns on contact.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

  • Laboratory sign kits
  • Gas cylinder sign kits

Common questions

Do these work with an oxygen monitor?

Yes. Post them next to the monitor and alarm, so people know what the alarm means.

Do you make dewar handling signs?

Yes, and we make custom versions too.

title: Chlorine and Hypochlorite Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At the chlorine or hypochlorite feed room door.
  • At the bulk fill connection, so a delivery driver never connects acid to the hypochlorite line.
  • At cylinder and ton container storage.
  • At ventilation and leak alarm controls.

Why mixing is the big one

Mixing sodium hypochlorite with an acid releases chlorine gas. Many plant incidents start at a fill connection where two chemicals are delivered side by side. A clear sign at each connection is a cheap safeguard.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

guide:
Where to post

  • At boiler and mechanical room doors.
  • At generator enclosures and exhaust outlets.

Carbon monoxide replaces oxygen in the blood. Early symptoms like headache and dizziness are easy to brush off, and people can become confused before they realize something is wrong.

title: Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At fermentation rooms and tank cellars.
  • At bulk CO2 tanks and beverage cylinder storage, especially in basements.
  • At rooms protected by CO2 fire suppression, with what to do when the alarm sounds.
  • At dry ice storage and shipping areas.

Why it matters

A leaking beverage CO2 tank in a basement or walk-in can build up to dangerous levels with no smell. Total-flooding CO2 fire suppression is designed to remove oxygen from a room, which is why NFPA 12 calls for warning signs at those spaces.

Signing a whole site?

Our kits put every sign one area needs in a single order, priced below buying the same signs one at a time.

title: Hydrofluoric Acid (HF) Signs
guide:
Where to post

  • At HF storage and use areas, including fume hoods and wet benches.
  • Next to the calcium gluconate first aid kit and the emergency shower.
  • At waste collection points.

Why it is different

Unlike most acids, HF passes through skin and attacks deeper tissue and bone, and it can affect the heart by pulling calcium from the blood. Exposure needs immediate first aid and medical care even when the burn looks small.

  • Next to the calcium gluconate first aid kit and the emergency shower.
  • At waste collection points.

Why it is different

Unlike most acids, HF passes through skin and attacks deeper tissue and bone, and it can affect the heart by pulling calcium from the blood. Exposure needs immediate first aid and medical care even when the burn looks small.

title: Call 811 Before Digging Signs
guide:
Where buried utility signs go

  • Along pipeline and cable routes, at road crossings, fence lines and property corners.

Locators mark buried lines with the APWA uniform color code: red for electric, yellow for gas and oil, orange for communications, blue for potable water, green for sewer and drain, purple for reclaimed water, pink for temporary survey marks and white for proposed excavation. A permanent sign tells people a line is there even after the paint is gone.

title: Confined Space Signs
guide:
The one sign OSHA spells out

Under OSHA 1910.146(c)(2), an employer with permit-required confined spaces must inform exposed employees by posting danger signs or another equally effective means. The standard gives the example language: DANGER, PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER.

Where to post

  • At every entry: manholes, vaults, tanks, pits, silos, wet wells and boilers.
  • On hatches that are opened from the top, where the sign may need to face up.
  • At the entry permit board, so the permit is easy to find.

title: OSHA Regulated Area Signs
guide:
What a regulated area is

Several OSHA substance-specific standards, including those for asbestos, lead, benzene, methylene chloride, cadmium and others, require the employer to set up regulated areas where exposure can exceed the permissible limit and to post them with specific warning wording.

Getting the wording right

Each standard lists its own legend, and several were updated when OSHA aligned them with the Hazard Communication Standard. Our regulated area signs use the wording the current standard specifies. If you need one we do not list, we will make it as a custom sign.

title: Arc Flash Signs
guide:
Where arc flash signs go

  • On switchboards, panelboards, motor control centers and meter sockets likely to be worked on while energized.
  • At electrical room doors.
  • At disconnects and transfer switches.

Standards to know

NEC 110.16 requires field marking to warn qualified persons of potential arc flash hazards on equipment likely to be examined, adjusted, serviced or maintained while energized. NFPA 70E covers the arc flash risk assessment and the equipment labels that list incident energy or PPE category. Our signs are the general warnings, not the calculated equipment labels from a study.
